deep.reconstruction:
This page is a draft of a historical and terminological preamble titled 'On the expressions: convergence [and] infinite series'. It is most likely related to the historical part of Riemann's 1854 Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series, or to lectures on convergence. The previous page's upside-down notes refer to 'Ueber Convergenz' and Art. 15–16 of a Diss.

(1) Methodological thesis. Neither 'convergence' nor 'infinite series' is used with a fixed meaning in the literature. If the meaning of 'infinite series' changes, the meaning of 'convergence' must change with it. So one must first fix what an infinite series is.

(2) Historical claim: the merit of introducing infinite series belongs to Newton, through 'De analysi per aequationes numero terminorum infinitas'.
- It was first printed in 1711 by W. Jones, as part of 'Analysis per quantitatum series, fluxiones ac differentias'.
- Jones's preface argues from the Collins correspondence (later printed at the Society's expense, i.e. the Commercium epistolicum, 1712) that Newton had the method by 1666. This would be two years before Mercator's Logarithmotechnia (1668), which also contains an infinite series. The marginal addition says the method was found and the work written before 1668.

(3) Textual argument. In Newton's tract 'infinite series' means simply a sum with infinitely many terms. Riemann quotes p. 7: 'Vel si ponas sqrt(x-xx)=y, erit radix aequalis infinitae seriei' (he stresses: not 'summae infinitae seriei') of the terms x^(1/2), -1/2 x^(3/2), -1/8 x^(5/2), ..., namely
  y = x^(1/2) - (1/2)x^(3/2) - (1/8)x^(5/2) - (1/16)x^(7/2) - (5/128)x^(9/2) - ...
This is, implicitly (my addition), sqrt(x)·(1-x)^(1/2) expanded by the binomial series. He also quotes p. 8: 'Ex hisce, credo, satis patebit modus reducendi quemlibet valorem ipsius y in series infinitas simplicium terminorum.'

(4) Proposed meaning of convergence. If an infinite series means a formation of sums that can be continued indefinitely (partial sums), then convergence naturally means the following. The further one continues, the narrower the 'Spielraum' (range) of its values becomes, and the bounding interval contains all later values. In modern terms: let I_N be the smallest interval containing {S_n : n ≥ N}. Then I_N shrinks to zero length, i.e. sup_{m,n≥N} |S_m - S_n| → 0. This is the Cauchy criterion, phrased as nested oscillation intervals.

(5) Closing remark: this use of the word 'infinite series' (identifying it with its sum or value) is hardly idiomatic. Yet this careless usage is found in all later writings of the [last] century.
errors: Historical: De analysi was actually written in 1669 (sent via Barrow to Collins), i.e. after Mercator's Logarithmotechnia (1668). Riemann's '1666' repeats the priority claim of Jones and the Commercium epistolicum, which concerns Newton's possession of the method, not the writing of the tract. The marginal correction 'vor 1668' is also only a claim from the priority dispute.

Historical: crediting Newton with introducing infinite series ignores earlier work (Madhava school, Gregory, Mercator, Wallis, Brouncker). This was a common 19th-century view, not a slip in the mathematics.
The series itself is correct: the binomial coefficients 1, -1/2, -1/8, -1/16, -5/128 for (1-x)^(1/2) check out.

results.what: Binomial series expansion sqrt(x-x^2) = x^(1/2) - x^(3/2)/2 - x^(5/2)/8 - x^(7/2)/16 - 5x^(9/2)/128 - ..., quoted from Newton
Convergence defined as the shrinking of the interval containing all later partial sums (range of values narrows to zero)
results.modern_name: Cauchy convergence criterion / oscillation of partial sums tending to 0

results.what: Historical-terminological remark that 'infinite series' was used as synonymous with its sum, and that the meaning of convergence depends on the meaning of series

deep.surprise_reason: This is a historical and terminological draft with a correct standard binomial expansion and a verbal Cauchy-type definition of convergence. It fits Riemann's known historical interest in the Habilitationsschrift and contains nothing new mathematically.
transcription_corrections: The right margin near the Newton paragraph carries an alternative opening, roughly 'Es gebührt ihm [die] Anwendung der [-unendlichen Reihen-] in der Analysis in dem ...'. It is missing from the machine transcription.
The last series term is x^(9/2) (the superscript is partly hidden in the image as 'x^2'); the coefficient -1/8 for x^(5/2) is correct despite the blot.
'(welcher später auf Kosten der Soc. herausgegeben wurde)' probably reads 'auf Kosten der Soc. Reg.' (Royal Society, Commercium epistolicum 1712).
In the last line 'des vorigen Jahrh.', 'vorigen' appears struck or overwritten; the sense is 'all later writings of the [18th] century'.
